name: Pasta Alla Gricia
headnote: Sasha Marx, who grew up in Rome, writes this as a defence of the least famous of the city's four classic pastas, which is usually dismissed as a white amatriciana or an eggless carbonara. With only pork, pepper, pasta and cheese in play, he insists on guanciale rather than pancetta for its funk, and on bronze-die pasta, which leaches more starch and holds sauce better than Teflon-extruded supermarket brands; the guanciale is cut into lardons, rendered slowly over medium-low heat so the fat comes out before the meat burns, then lifted out so it stays crisp, and the pepper is bloomed in the rendered fat. The pasta boils in only three quarts of water for a starchier broth and comes out at five minutes, badly undercooked, to finish in the skillet with two cups of that water, constantly swirled so it keeps shedding starch, builds the emulsion and glazes itself. The pecorino goes in off the heat in two additions so it does not clump or break the sauce.
comment_digest: The most detailed critique comes from a cook who found the dish far too salty and over-porked: he says two cups of pasta water was too much, that he had to lift the par-cooked rigatoni out and reduce the sauce separately to stop it overcooking, that his sauce turned an unappealing tan despite rendering slowly, and that he would cut the guanciale, the water and the cheese. Cooks scaling up report the opposite ratio, needing roughly 2.5 to 3 cups of pasta water for a full pound of rigatoni, with one saying he would go lower next time for a drier result. One skips salting the pasta water entirely here and seasons at the table, and substitutes diced pancetta where jowl is unavailable, reporting both fresh and dried pasta work. Guanciale's cost is a recurring objection, and one reviewer felt the skillet finish added no depth for the extra active time.
flags: Thinner comment section than the other pages: 28 reviews, only nine of which carried a star rating, and no 'Featured Tweaks' block. Comments truncated at 'Read More'.
